title: Diary Entry About Rainy Day: 5 Examples for Students
description: Diary entry about rainy day: 5 model entries for kids and class 6 to 10, the right format, rain words and phrases, and a free diary page to write your own.
h1: Diary entry about a rainy day (5 examples)
intro: A diary entry about a rainy day gives the date and day, starts with **Dear Diary**, describes the rain with your senses (sound, smell, sight, touch), tells what you did, and says how the weather made you feel. Below are 5 complete model entries, from a short one for young kids to longer ones for older students, plus rain words, steps and a page to write your own.

writer.title: Dear diary,
writer.hint: It rained all day today. I...

blocks.p: A rainy day entry uses the normal diary layout. What makes it special is description. Examiners love to see that you can paint the weather with words, not just say "it rained".

ul: **Date, day and time** at the top, for example: Saturday, 12 July, 7 p.m.
**Opening:** what the sky and the rain were like when the day began.
**Middle:** what you did because of the rain, written in the past tense.
**Feelings:** cozy, gloomy, playful, bored, peaceful. Say why.
**Closing and name**, such as Good night, then your name.

blocks.tip: Try to use at least three senses. What did the rain sound like on the roof? What did the air smell like? How cold were the drops?

sections.h2: Short diary entry about a rainy day (for kids)

blocks.p: About 80 words. Simple sentences, one happy activity and a cozy ending. Good for grades 2 to 5.

example.label: Short entry
example.title: Dear Diary,
example.text:
It rained all day today! The sky was gray and the rain
went tap, tap, tap on my window.
After lunch, Mom said I could go outside in my yellow
rain boots. I jumped in every puddle on our street.
The biggest one splashed right up to my knees!
When I came inside, my socks were soaking wet.
We made hot cocoa and watched a movie under a blanket.
Rainy days are the coziest days.
Love,
Zoe

blocks.p: Look at the sound word (tap, tap, tap), the color (gray sky, yellow boots) and the clear feeling at the end. Three small touches make a short entry feel complete.

sections.h2: Diary entry about rainy day in 120 to 150 words

blocks.p: This exam style model is the right length for most class 6 to 10 papers. It describes the first rain of the monsoon.

example.label: Exam style
example.title: Dear Diary,
example.text:
Today the monsoon finally arrived. For weeks the heat had
been unbearable, but this afternoon dark clouds rolled in
and the sky rumbled like a giant drum.
Within minutes, heavy drops began to fall. The dry earth
gave off a sweet, muddy smell that I love more than any
perfume. My little brother and I ran to the balcony and
held out our hands to catch the cool water.
Grandma fried hot pakoras, and we sat together watching
the street turn into a small river. We made paper boats
from old notebook pages and sent them sailing below.
Mine sank, but my brother's floated all the way to the
corner shop.
I felt fresh and happy for the first time in weeks.
The rain washed away the dust and my bad mood too.
Good night,
Ananya

blocks.p: Why it works: a clear before and after (heat, then relief), a smell, a sound, a family moment, and one small funny detail with the paper boats. It also ends with a feeling, which is what a diary is for.
These longer models show three very different rainy days. Use them for ideas on creative writing tasks, or to see how older students add depth.

blocks.h3: Stuck indoors with a power cut

example.label: Longer entry
example.title: Dear Diary,
example.text:
The rain started before I woke up and did not stop once.
It beat against the windows so hard that Dad joked we
should start building an ark.
At about two o'clock there was a huge crack of thunder,
and the lights went out. No Wi-Fi, no TV, no charger.
At first I sulked on the sofa. Then Mum found candles
and an old box of board games in the cupboard.
We played Monopoly by candlelight for three hours. My
sister bought every station and was unbearable about it.
Dad told stories about storms when he was a boy, and we
ate cold sandwiches because the cooker would not work.
The power came back at seven, and everyone groaned.
It is strange, but I think the best part of the weekend
was the part with no electricity.
Night night,
Oliver

example.label: Longer entry
example.title: Dear Diary,
example.text:
We had our big match against the school down the road
today, and of course a summer storm arrived right at
kickoff. Thunder rolled over the hills, and in five
minutes the field turned into chocolate pudding.
Coach said we could stop, but nobody wanted to go home.
We slid, we fell, and the ball kept stopping dead in
the puddles. I could hardly see through the rain.
In the last minute, the ball bounced off Musa's knee
and rolled to me. I kicked it with everything I had.
It skidded through the mud and over the line. Goal!
We won 1 to 0. My kit is so muddy that Mama made me
wash it outside with the hose. I don't even care.
Best rainy day ever,
Lwazi

blocks.p: Not every rainy day entry has to be cheerful. This one, for older students, uses the rain to show a mood.

example.label: Reflective entry
example.title: Dear Diary,
example.text:
It has been drizzling since lunch, the soft kind of rain
that never quite stops. The sky stayed the color of wet
concrete all afternoon.
I sat by my window after school and watched the drops
race each other down the glass. I picked one and cheered
for it in my head. Silly, I know.
I think the rain made me miss Hana more. This is the first
spring since she moved away, and last year we walked home
together under one umbrella every rainy day.
So tonight I wrote her a real letter, on paper, with a
drawing of our old bus stop. I will post it tomorrow.
The rain is still falling as I write this. It sounds
gentle now, almost like it is keeping me company.
Good night,
Mei

sections.h2: Words and phrases to describe a rainy day

head: Sense
Words
Phrases
rows: gray, gloomy, misty, overcast, puddles, rainbow
dark clouds rolled in, the street turned into a river
rain drummed on the tin roof, thunder rumbled in the distance
the sweet smell of wet soil, the air smelled clean
soaked to the skin, cold drops ran down my neck
cozy, peaceful, gloomy, playful, bored, refreshed
the rain washed away my bad mood, I felt snug indoors

ul: Light rain: drizzle, sprinkle, shower, spitting
Heavy rain: downpour, cloudburst, torrential rain, raining cats and dogs
Storm words: thunderstorm, lightning flashed, gusty wind, hailstones
After the rain: dripping leaves, a fresh breeze, a rainbow over the rooftops

blocks.p: For more weather and nature ideas, see our list of [diary entry topics](/diary-entry-topics/).

sections.h2: How to write your own diary entry about a rainy day

steps.name: Put the date, day and time at the top
steps.text: Add Dear Diary on the next line.

steps.name: Open with the weather
steps.text: Describe the sky or the first drops in one or two sentences. Use one sound or color word.

steps.name: Tell what you did because of the rain
steps.text: Stayed in, played outside, got caught on the way home, watched from the window. Keep it in the past tense.

steps.name: Add your senses
steps.text: Pick at least three: what you saw, heard, smelled and felt.

steps.name: Say how the rain made you feel
steps.text: Happy, cozy, bored, thoughtful. Give a reason.

steps.name: Close warmly
steps.text: End with a final thought, a closing like Good night, and your name.

blocks.p: Tap a card to start a page in the diary at the top. Need a refresher on layout first? Read our [diary entry format](/diary-entry-format/) guide or [how to write a diary entry](/how-to-write-a-diary-entry/).

sections.h2: Common mistakes in rainy day diary entries

ul: **Only saying "it rained".** Describe it. How hard? What sound? What smell?
**Forgetting yourself.** It is a diary, not a weather report. Tell what you did and felt.
**Mixing tenses.** Keep the events in the past: it rained, we played, I felt.
**Missing the date or name.** These are part of the format and usually carry marks.
**Too many big words at once.** One strong word like drenched is better than five fancy ones in a row.
**No ending.** Finish with a feeling or a thought, not just the last event.

blocks.p: Want more model answers? See our [diary entry examples](/diary-entry-examples/), or try a happy one like this [diary entry about summer vacation](/diary-entry-about-summer-vacation/). Kids who enjoy writing can keep going with our [journal prompts for kids](/journal-prompts-for-kids/).

faq.q: How do I describe a rainy day in a diary entry?
faq.a: Use your senses. Say what the sky looked like, what the rain sounded like on the roof or window, how the wet earth smelled, and how the drops felt on your skin. Then add what you did and how it made you feel. One sound word, one smell and one feeling are enough to bring a short entry to life.

faq.q: How do you start a diary entry about a rainy day?
faq.a: Write the date, day and time, then Dear Diary. Your first line can set the scene, for example: Today the sky turned dark gray just after lunch, and soon the rain was drumming on our roof. Starting with the weather straight away tells the reader what the entry is about.

faq.q: What can I write if nothing happened on the rainy day?
faq.a: Write about the small things. What did you watch from the window? What did you eat? Who did you talk to? Did you read, draw, sleep or feel bored? A quiet day can make a lovely diary entry if you describe the mood and your thoughts honestly.

faq.q: How long should a diary entry about a rainy day be?
faq.a: Follow the word limit in your question. For most class 6 to 10 exams it is about 100 to 150 words. Younger children can write 60 to 100 words. Creative writing homework can be longer, around 200 to 300 words, with more description and feelings.

faq.q: Is a rainy day diary entry written in past or present tense?
faq.a: Mainly the past tense, because you are writing about what happened earlier today: it rained, we played, I felt cozy. If it is still raining as you write, you can use the present tense for that one moment, such as The rain is still falling as I write this.
